tone_statements.citation: Stanford, Ronald. 1967. The Bekwarra language of Nigeria: a grammatical description. PhD thesis, School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. 326 pp. (ProQuest 10673020 digitisation; CORE mirror of SOAS Research Online)
tone_statements.quote: The basic tone-bearing unit is the syllabic, syllables (with a few special exceptions) being of the pattern CV (consonant - vowel), V (vowel) or N (syllabic nasal). Each of these normally bears a single unit of tone, viz. high, mid or low (abbreviated H, M and L respectively). … When the tone associated with a non-word-initial V or N syllable differs from that of a preceding syllable (which must be of structure CV) the two tones together are realised as a rising or falling pitch extending over the two syllables …

tone.quote: The basic tone-bearing unit is the syllabic, syllables (with a few special exceptions) being of the pattern CV (consonant - vowel), V (vowel) or N (syllabic nasal). Each of these normally bears a single unit of tone, viz. high, mid or low (abbreviated H, M and L respectively). … When the tone associated with a non-word-initial V or N syllable differs from that of a preceding syllable (which must be of structure CV) the two tones together are realised as a rising or falling pitch extending over the two syllables …
tone.says: Three level tones, high, mid and low, one on each syllable (CV, V or syllabic nasal); rising and falling glides analysed as sequences of two level tones; verbs fall into H, M and L tone classes.

sources.note: Segmental phonology and processes only (25 consonants vs Stanford's 22 and Robert 2018's 28; five vowels, no length, no ATR harmony; assimilation, vowel elision, coalescence, insertion in loans). Tone is NOT described: the single tone remark is in the abstract, rejecting Robert's long vowels -- what Robert heard as length is high tone ('The language only has high tone instead of long vowels'). Data are tone-marked with acute/grave accents throughout but no inventory, count or tonal process is given; the conclusion calls for 'more research on Békwarra phonology'.
